title: SaaS Industry Statistics 2026
description: Essential statistics on the SaaS industry including market size, growth metrics, pricing trends, churn benchmarks, and public company performance.

sections.title: Market Size and Growth
sections.body: The SaaS market stands at $317 billion in 2026, growing 18.4% year over year on the strength of cloud migration, AI functionality, and new category creation, with forecasts reaching $525 billion by 2030. SaaS has become the default delivery model for enterprise software: 64% of enterprise software is now delivered as a service, while remaining on-premises and hybrid deployments shrink 8% annually as vendors end support for self-hosted editions. Geographically, North America still generates 47% of SaaS revenue, but Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region at a 26% CAGR, reflecting the enterprise digitization wave in India, Southeast Asia, and Japan. For buyers, the on-prem decline matters at renewal time — legacy suites without viable SaaS pathways are becoming stranded investment, so license reviews should score vendor SaaS migration paths as heavily as current pricing.

sections.title: Pricing and Revenue Metrics
sections.body: Pricing is where SaaS economics are shifting fastest in 2026. Usage-based pricing is now the dominant model for new products — 73% of SaaS companies offer it, and 42% of new products launch with it — while established vendors increasingly run hybrid pricing that layers consumption, per-seat, and AI surcharge components. The cost side is moving against buyers: average per-seat prices rose 14% year over year, 67% of vendors now add AI feature surcharges averaging $25 per user per month, and average annual contract discounts have tightened to 15% as vendors prioritize predictable recurring revenue over upfront acquisition volume. The practical implication is that contract benchmarks from two years ago understate today's effective price, and usage-based clauses for AI features — what counts as a credit, how consumption spikes are billed, and whether discounts compound with volume — have become the negotiation battleground for renewals.

sections.title: Retention and Churn Benchmarks
sections.body: Retention separates the SaaS leaders from the crowded middle. Top-quartile public companies hold 92% net revenue retention — meaning expansion revenue from existing customers replaces nearly everything churned — while the median company trails far behind. Gross churn tells the same story by segment: median monthly churn is 5.2% among SMB customers versus just 1.8% in enterprise, the gap reflecting the deeper integration, contracts, and switching costs of large accounts. The most instructive movement in 2026 is in AI software specifically: annual retention improved from 76% in 2024 to 84% in 2026 as AI tools moved from novelty experiments to embedded daily workflows. For buyers, churn benchmarks are a useful health signal when evaluating private vendors — a 5%-plus monthly SMB churn with weak expansion indicates a product that sells but does not retain.

sections.title: Public SaaS Company Performance
sections.body: Public SaaS performance has re-stabilized around durable economics: the median company trades at 7.8x enterprise value to revenue after the post-2021 correction, generates 65% gross margins, and has pushed median EBITDA margins to 24% — a profitability bar that disciplined growth models now fund marketing and sales from. The efficiency shift is visible in the IPO pipeline: companies now reach a median $12.4 million ARR before going public, roughly double the threshold of the boom years, and 38% of public SaaS companies already generate more than half their revenue through self-serve channels without a salesperson touching the customer. The read-through for software buyers is that vendors with 65%-plus gross margins and self-serve revenue have the room to compete on price — while low-margin vendors with heavy sales costs are the ones most likely to raise prices or cap feature access in coming renewals.
